summary: In SQLite write-ahead logging, a checkpoint copies committed frames from the WAL into the main database, allowing the WAL to be reused and keeping recovery and reads manageable. SQLite normally runs passive auto-checkpoints at a configurable page threshold, currently documented as 1000 pages by default. Passive checkpoints do not wait for readers or writers and may stop before completion. A reader holding an older snapshot can prevent a checkpoint from advancing past that reader's end mark, so sustained overlapping reads can delay WAL reset and permit growth. FULL, RESTART, and TRUNCATE modes wait more aggressively; TRUNCATE additionally reduces the WAL file to zero bytes after successful completion. Checkpoint frequency trades write latency against WAL size and read costs, so the default is a policy choice rather than a fixed best setting for every workload.

claims.text: A checkpoint copies committed WAL content back into the main database; SQLite's normal checkpoint process preserves the committed database state while moving those page changes out of the log.

SQLite documents automatic checkpointing at 1000 WAL pages by default, triggered by a commit that reaches the threshold; the threshold can be changed or auto-checkpointing disabled. The current pragma documentation was updated 2026-10-04.

Automatic checkpoints use PASSIVE mode. A passive checkpoint does as much work as possible without waiting for readers or writers, and can leave frames uncheckpointed when concurrent activity prevents completion.

A reader holding an older WAL snapshot can prevent a checkpoint from advancing beyond that reader's end mark; persistent overlapping readers can therefore prevent completion and WAL reset, allowing the WAL to grow without bound.

A successful checkpoint usually recycles the WAL for reuse rather than truncating it, so a large on-disk WAL file alone does not show that no frames were checkpointed; TRUNCATE mode reduces the file to zero bytes only after successful completion.

SQLite distinguishes FULL, RESTART, and TRUNCATE checkpoint modes: FULL waits for writers and readers to reach the latest snapshot and blocks new writers; RESTART also waits until readers no longer use the WAL; TRUNCATE adds zero-length truncation on success.

The APSW Python wrapper exposes Connection.wal_checkpoint(dbname, mode), defaults the mode to PASSIVE, and returns WAL frame and checkpointed-frame counts, providing a wrapper-level way to invoke and inspect SQLite checkpointing.

sources.title: SQLite/SSL: A SQLite-Based DBMS for Flash Storage

open_questions: The best checkpoint interval depends on workload and storage latency; the sources do not prescribe a universally optimal threshold.
